abstract:
Establishing peer-to-peer UDP connections across Network Address Translation (NAT) boundaries is a persistent challenge in networked applications. This C library addresses that problem by providing a simplified implementation of the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) protocol, enabling bidirectional UDP streams with NAT traversal without requiring external dependencies.

The library implements both client-side and server-side ICE agent functionality conforming to RFC 8445, with support for STUN (RFC 8489), TURN relaying (RFC 8656), TCP candidates (RFC 6544), ICE consent freshness (RFC 7675), and an SDP-based interface (RFC 8839). It supports IPv4/IPv6 dual-stack operation and optional multiplexing on a single UDP port. A lightweight embedded STUN/TURN server is also included and can be disabled at compile time.

The design deliberately trades completeness for simplicity: only UDP transport is supported, and each session handles a single component—sufficient for use cases such as WebRTC Data Channels and multiplexed RTP/RTCP. The library is written in C with no mandatory dependencies, making it portable across GNU/Linux, Android, FreeBSD, macOS, iOS, and Windows. An optional integration with the Nettle cryptography library can substitute the internal HMAC-SHA1 and SHA-256 implementations. Build support is provided via CMake and Make, with language bindings available for Rust.

A macOS application addresses the absence of a native "Active Desktop" feature on the platform — a capability that allows users to display live, interactive web content as their desktop wallpaper, historically available on Windows but not macOS. The approach involves rendering any user-specified website directly onto the desktop background layer, turning the wallpaper into a dynamic, web-powered surface rather than a static image. Technically, the application is built in Swift and leverages macOS system APIs to position a web view at the lowest window layer, behind all other application windows but above the standard desktop. It uses a modern UserDefaults wrapper for persistent settings storage and supports user-customizable global keyboard shortcuts for controlling behavior without foregrounding the application. The result is a persistent, always-visible web layer that can display anything a browser can render — dashboards, clocks, visualizations, or any arbitrary web page — updating in real time as the underlying content changes. Configuration is managed through a menu bar interface, allowing users to specify URLs and adjust display parameters. The tool is distributed as a closed-source macOS application, with issue tracking maintained publicly for bug reports and feature requests.

This project implements a cellular automaton-based evolution simulator inspired by Conway's Game of Life, designed to model natural selection through emergent behavioral evolution. The core problem it addresses is simulating how simple genetic rules can give rise to evolutionary dynamics in a grid-based environment.

Each entity in the simulation occupies a cell on a two-dimensional grid and carries a directional state along with a pointer to a genome — a lookup table of 256 entries mapping every possible neighborhood configuration (based on which of the eight surrounding cells are occupied) to one of three behaviors: move forward into an empty cell, turn left or right, or reproduce. Reproduction requires a living cell ahead and an empty cell behind; the forward neighbor is consumed, and an offspring is placed behind the parent facing the opposite direction. A small per-reproduction mutation probability allows offspring to inherit modified genomes, enabling evolutionary divergence over time.

The simulator is a command-line tool supporting configurable world dimensions, population sizes, random seeds, frame rates, and periodic save intervals. Worlds can be serialized to and loaded from binary files in a custom format, with a provided migration script for converting between format versions. Optional graphical output renders the simulation in real time. A custom file-magic descriptor is included to enable system-level file type recognition of the world format.

A standard bump allocator offers very fast allocation by simply advancing a pointer into a memory segment, but it cannot reclaim memory for arbitrary free patterns, leading to unbounded growth. This implementation addresses that limitation with a modified bump allocator that supports partial memory reclamation by tracking freed regions at the top of the allocation stack. When the most recently allocated block is freed, the allocator walks backward through contiguously freed blocks and reclaims them all, collapsing the stack pointer. This allows stack-disciplined allocation patterns — where memory is freed in roughly reverse-allocation order — to avoid leaking, even without a full general-purpose allocator. The implementation compiles to a shared library and can be injected into existing processes via dynamic linker preload mechanisms (`LD_PRELOAD` on Linux, `DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES` on macOS), replacing the system allocator transparently. It implements the full standard allocation interface including `malloc`, `calloc`, `realloc`, `free`, `aligned_alloc`, `posix_memalign`, and related functions. Memory is obtained from the OS via `brk`. Compilation options allow configuring allocation alignment (required to be a power of two), `errno` propagation, and single-threaded mode that removes mutex locking overhead. The codebase is written in ANSI C, with minimal platform-specific code needed for porting. The authors note the allocator is slower than system allocators in benchmarks and is not recommended for production use.

This project addresses the challenge of understanding para-virtualized device implementation by providing a concrete, fully reproducible educational example using QEMU and Linux on an AArch64 architecture. Para-virtualization involves a guest operating system cooperating with a hypervisor through explicit interfaces rather than hardware emulation, and implementing such devices requires coordinating host-side device logic, guest kernel drivers, and userland interfaces simultaneously.

The approach demonstrates all three layers through a stopwatch application: timekeeping logic runs inside the QEMU host process as a virtual device, while a Linux kernel module serves as the guest driver, and shell scripts in the guest userland provide the user interface. The virtual device exposes three hardware-visible resources — a trapping memory region (where guest accesses trigger host-side callbacks), a pass-through memory region (direct memory sharing), and an interrupt line — all described to the guest kernel via a Device Tree Blob. The guest driver discovers these resources through DTB parsing and exposes control interfaces via sysfs and debugfs virtual files.

The build system automates downloading, patching, and compiling QEMU, Linux, and BusyBox from source, then assembles a minimal root filesystem and launches the virtual machine. Patches integrate the custom device into QEMU's build system and the driver into the Linux kernel tree. The entire stack can be reproduced with a single make invocation, optionally inside a Docker container for dependency isolation.

A curated directory addresses the challenge of coordinating disparate volunteer software efforts and research resources during the COVID-19 pandemic by consolidating them into a single, collaboratively maintained reference list. The approach is community-driven curation: contributors aggregate open-source projects, data repositories, and authoritative public health references into a structured document that can be incrementally extended by anyone with relevant knowledge.

Technically, the collection is organized into three categories. The first covers active software tools, including geographic testing-site mapping applications, web-based pre-screening and risk-assessment tools, epidemiological outbreak trajectory modeling systems, distributed protein-folding simulations for coronavirus research, REST and GraphQL APIs wrapping publicly available case data from a major academic epidemiology repository, and statistical dashboards. The second category provides links to foundational datasets and analytical resources, including genomic surveillance pipelines, disease modeling parameter repositories, and official guidance from international and national public health bodies. The third section identifies open technical and logistical problems still seeking solutions, such as community supply-sharing platforms and economic support mechanisms for affected individuals.

The repository itself functions as a lightweight coordination layer—a plain markdown document maintained via standard version-control contribution workflows—allowing distributed contributors to surface projects needing assistance without requiring centralized infrastructure or gatekeeping.

A common challenge in C and C++ development is integrating unit tests without requiring a separate test harness infrastructure or significant boilerplate. This framework addresses that gap by allowing tests to be embedded directly alongside the code under test, with minimal setup required beyond including a header file.

The approach centers on two components: a header file that defines test-writing macros, and a companion executable that discovers and runs tests by inspecting compiled binaries. Tests are defined using macros that generate static functions containing arbitrary C statements and assertions. For C99 and later, a conditional compilation symbol controls whether test code is included in the build; for ANSI C (C89), an alternative header is provided with a slightly different macro syntax requiring an explicit return value and manual conditional compilation guards.

Technically, the runner executable leverages the POSIX `nm` utility to locate test symbols in a compiled binary, then invokes each discovered test function, capturing output and monitoring for failures via signals or assertion aborts. The system targets POSIX.1-2001 compliant environments. Output is deliberately kept plain-text and line-oriented to facilitate downstream processing with standard Unix tools such as `awk`, `grep`, and `sed`, for which several example pipelines are provided. Tests must be compiled with exported symbols, potentially requiring shared library compilation flags. The framework requires no test registration code beyond the macro definitions themselves.

A command-line utility addresses the common need among systems programmers and storage engineers to perform byte-level arithmetic, unit conversion, and low-level address calculations without switching between multiple tools. The tool provides a REPL and single-execution CLI interface written in C, depending only on standard libc and optionally GNU Readline or BSD Editline for interactive input.

The approach combines storage-specific computation with general-purpose arithmetic in a unified interface. For storage operations, the tool evaluates arithmetic expressions involving SI and IEC binary-prefixed units (e.g., GiB, kB), converts between those units, computes byte addresses, and handles LBA/CHS conversions with configurable sector size, heads-per-cylinder, and sectors-per-track parameters. Expressions support addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, modulo, and bitwise operators including shifts, AND, OR, XOR, and complement.

General-purpose mode extends the tool with floating-point arithmetic and mathematical functions including exponentiation, logarithms, roots, and summation. Base conversion between binary, decimal, and hexadecimal is supported, along with bit-position visualization. Internally, the tool uses 128-bit unsigned integers when the compiler provides `__uint128_t`, falling back to 64-bit, while floating-point operations use `long double` precision. The REPL stores the last valid result in a reusable variable, supports piped input and file redirection, and maintains a history file following XDG Base Directory conventions.

A C library addresses the challenge of building cross-platform graphical user interfaces for desktop applications using familiar web development paradigms without requiring a full browser runtime. The approach integrates a subset of web frontend technologies—CSS styling, JSX syntax, TypeScript, and React-like component patterns—into a lightweight native C framework targeting Windows and Linux.

Technically, the system is composed of modular sub-libraries: a graphics layer handling font management, text layout, image processing, and 2D rendering; a CSS parser and selector engine for style computation; a platform abstraction layer providing message loops, window management, timers, and input method handling; and a core UI library managing component trees, event queues, style resolution, and drawing. A command-line build tool preprocesses TypeScript/JSX configuration files and generates corresponding C source code and resource files, enabling developers to describe component structure, state, data bindings, and event handlers declaratively before compiling to native code. Routing is handled through a filesystem-based router where directory structure maps to application pages. Stylesheet authoring supports utility-class frameworks, CSS modules, preprocessors, and global CSS. Components are fully custom-drawn to ensure visual consistency across platforms, with automatic DPI scaling for high-resolution displays. The architecture deliberately keeps the runtime small and dependency-light, trading feature completeness—such as a built-in animation system and rich component library—for a minimal footprint suitable for small desktop application projects.

A pure C implementation of the WebRTC protocol stack addresses the challenge of enabling real-time peer-to-peer audio and video communication on resource-constrained embedded and IoT devices where higher-level language runtimes are impractical. The library implements the full WebRTC specification in C, targeting portability across Linux, macOS, x64, and ARMv5 architectures with a compiled library footprint under 200 kilobytes.

Technically, the implementation covers the complete WebRTC protocol suite: ICE for NAT traversal with STUN and TURN support across IPv4 and IPv6, DTLS-SRTP for encrypted media transport, and RTP/RTCP for media delivery including NACK-based retransmission, congestion control callbacks, and FIR/PLI signaling. Supported codecs include VP8, H.264, Opus, and G.711 PCM in both A-law and µ-law variants. DataChannels are implemented via libusrsctp, and a bundled signaling client handles session negotiation over WebSockets using libwebsockets. The build system uses CMake and supports cross-compilation by exposing platform configuration flags; dependencies including OpenSSL or MBedTLS, libsrtp2, libjsmn, libusrsctp, and libwebsockets can either be built from source automatically or linked against system installations. An optional thread pool and runtime ICE statistics controls allow further tuning for constrained environments. The library exposes raw media input/output callbacks, giving developers direct control over the media pipeline without requiring an intermediate media framework.
